data.name: Frontline : Longest Day
data.detailed_description:
June 6th, 1944. D-Day is the Allied operation that launched the successful liberation of German-occupied Western Europe during World War II.

In Frontline: The Longest Day, players command the Allied forces through some of the most famous battles of the war, freeing Europe from the hands of the German Army. The game takes place over five massive, engaging and challenging missions, all inspired by historical missions which took place during operation Overlord: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Cherbourg, Sword & Juno.

Players are faced with tough decisions and will have to think through the options to take advantage of terrain, use their combat techniques wisely and make sure they leverage the special ability of each unit to overcome the enemy and get Europe back in safe hands.

FEATURES


  • Land, and aerial combat: all units have strengths and weaknesses encouraging different uses, adding an extra strategic layer to the game. There are over 80 of them!
  • Units will upgrade throughout the game, based on combat success and experience. This will prove to be an extremely powerful tool to progress in the game providing the players with a personalized army depending on their style of play.
  • Complex combat mechanics and special abilities for all units such as: Flanking manoeuvres, encirclements, suppression, combat fatigue, penetration, deflection, removing landmines, artillery support, airstrikes, transport, sandbags, march, APCR ammunition, incendiary grenades, smoke grenades, artillery barrages, reinforce & resupply.
  • Maps are created to reflect the real terrain and their dramatic impact on the historical situation.

reviews.review:
Frontline: The Longest Day is a World War II turn-based strategy game developed by 88mm and published by Slitherine Ltd. that places players in command of Allied forces during one of the most important military operations in modern history. Rather than attempting to simulate the entirety of the Second World War, the game focuses specifically on the Normandy invasion and the battles that followed. This narrower scope allows it to concentrate on a pivotal campaign while delivering a strategy experience that balances accessibility with tactical depth. The result is a game that seeks to appeal both to newcomers interested in military strategy and to veterans looking for a straightforward historical wargame.

The campaign is built around the events surrounding D-Day and the Allied push into occupied France. Players take control of a variety of military formations as they attempt to secure beaches, break through German defenses, capture strategic locations, and maintain momentum against determined opposition. The historical setting immediately gives the game a sense of importance, as every mission represents part of a larger effort that ultimately helped shape the outcome of the war.

One of the game's most appealing qualities is its approachable design. Many historical wargames overwhelm players with enormous rulebooks, complex logistics systems, and intimidating interfaces. Frontline: The Longest Day takes a more welcoming approach. The mechanics are relatively easy to understand, allowing players to focus on tactical decisions rather than spending hours learning intricate systems. This accessibility makes the game an attractive entry point for those curious about turn-based military strategy.

The gameplay revolves around careful positioning and efficient use of military units. Infantry, armored vehicles, artillery, aircraft, and support units all play important roles on the battlefield. Success rarely comes from simply advancing toward objectives. Players must coordinate different unit types, exploit enemy weaknesses, and protect vulnerable forces. The combined-arms approach creates situations where thoughtful planning consistently outperforms reckless aggression.

A particularly enjoyable feature is the progression system applied to military units. Forces that survive engagements gain experience and become more effective over time. Veteran units can develop into valuable assets that players become reluctant to risk unnecessarily. This mechanic adds a sense of continuity throughout the campaign and encourages players to think beyond immediate victories. Preserving experienced troops becomes just as important as capturing objectives, creating meaningful long-term strategic decisions.

The game's combat mechanics include a respectable amount of tactical depth beneath their straightforward presentation. Flanking maneuvers, artillery bombardments, air support missions, suppression effects, supply considerations, and defensive positioning all influence battlefield outcomes. Players who take advantage of these systems will find significantly greater success than those who rely solely on direct attacks. While the game remains accessible, it still rewards careful planning and strategic thinking.

The variety of available units helps maintain engagement throughout the campaign. Tanks provide powerful offensive capabilities, infantry remains essential for capturing and holding territory, and artillery can soften enemy defenses before an assault begins. Air units introduce additional tactical possibilities by allowing players to strike targets beyond the reach of ground forces. Understanding how these different elements work together becomes a key part of mastering the game.

Terrain plays a major role in every battle. Open fields expose advancing troops to enemy fire, forests offer concealment, and fortified positions can dramatically alter the flow of combat. The maps encourage players to consider the environment carefully before making decisions. Advancing without regard for terrain often leads to unnecessary casualties, while proper use of defensive positions and natural cover can completely change the outcome of an engagement.

Visually, Frontline: The Longest Day favors functionality over spectacle. The top-down perspective provides a clear view of the battlefield, making it easy to evaluate positions and issue commands. Unit models and terrain details are relatively simple, but the presentation succeeds in conveying information efficiently. The visual design prioritizes strategic clarity, which is arguably more important than graphical sophistication in a turn-based wargame.

The historical focus adds considerable appeal for military enthusiasts. The campaign recreates famous operations associated with the Normandy invasion and subsequent Allied advances. While the game does not attempt to become a detailed historical simulation, it captures enough of the campaign's atmosphere to make players feel connected to the events being represented. Fans of World War II history will likely appreciate the effort to ground missions in real military operations.

Unfortunately, the game's accessibility occasionally comes at the expense of depth. Experienced wargamers may find some systems too simplified compared to more advanced strategy titles. The artificial intelligence can also be inconsistent, sometimes providing competent resistance while at other times making questionable tactical decisions. These issues prevent the game from reaching the same level as the genre's most respected classics.

Technical limitations and a somewhat dated presentation also affect the overall experience. The interface is functional but lacks the refinement found in more modern strategy games. Certain features feel basic by contemporary standards, and some players may find the overall package lacking polish. Community reception has been mixed over the years, reflecting both appreciation for the game's accessibility and criticism of its shortcomings.

Even with these flaws, Frontline: The Longest Day remains a competent and enjoyable strategy title. It succeeds at delivering a focused World War II campaign that is easy to understand while still offering meaningful tactical choices. The combination of historical scenarios, unit progression, combined-arms warfare, and accessible mechanics creates a satisfying experience for players interested in military strategy without requiring an overwhelming commitment.

For newcomers seeking an introduction to turn-based wargames, the game provides a solid starting point. More experienced strategy fans may find it less sophisticated than genre leaders, but there is still enjoyment to be found in its historical setting and tactical gameplay. While it does not redefine the genre, it offers a respectable and entertaining recreation of one of the most significant military campaigns of the twentieth century.

Rating: 5/10
